_about: Notes for photos that show a mineral in a less typical way. Keyed by the photo's source page; shown after the identification tip.
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:: This photo shows olivine as green grains stuck in a dark volcanic rock, a common way to find it in nature.
This piece is covered in green tarnish, which happens when copper sits in air and water for a long time. Look for the copper-colored metal peeking through.
This is a 'desert rose': gypsum blades that grew inside sand, so they're tan and gritty instead of clear. The thin, curved blades are the clue.
This clear piece of calcite (called Iceland spar) makes the words under it look doubled. That trick only works with clear calcite, and it's a great clue!
These are peridot, the gem name for olivine. They've been tumbled smooth and shiny, the way you'd find them in a rock shop. Rough olivine is grainier, but it's the same olive-green color.
